Keeping Your Hands Warm

Cold hands are the most common complaint of winter riders. At motorway speeds in winter, wind chill drives effective temperature well below minus 10 degrees Celsius. Without proper insulation, fingers become numb within minutes making throttle and brake control dangerously imprecise.

Why Hands Get Cold Quickly

Your hands are fully exposed at the front of the bike gripping metal controls that conduct cold. Blood flow to extremities reduces when core temperature drops. Unlike your torso, hands have minimal insulating body fat. These factors combine to make hand warming one of winter riding's biggest challenges.

What to Look For

  • Insulation — PrimaLoft, Thinsulate, or similar synthetics maintaining warmth when damp. Natural down is too fragile for motorcycle use.
  • Waterproofing — Essential as wet cold hands lose heat five times faster. Gore-Tex or equivalent membrane.
  • Gauntlet length — Long gauntlets sealing over jacket cuffs prevent wind tracking up sleeves.
  • Pre-curved fingers — Especially important in thick winter gloves to maintain dexterity on controls.
  • Visor wipe — Chamois or rubber strip on left index finger for clearing rain from your visor.

Best Winter Gloves 2026

Held Season Gore-Tex — Benchmark winter glove with Gore-Tex, PrimaLoft insulation, and kangaroo leather palm. Waterproof, warm, and excellent dexterity for thick winter construction.

Rukka Virium 2.0 GTX — Outstanding warmth with Gore-Tex Grip technology. Snug yet comfortable fit with touchscreen compatibility that actually works.

Rev It Stratos 3 GTX — Mid-price Gore-Tex winter glove with good insulation and comfortable gauntlet. Effective down to around minus 5 degrees.

Oxford Mondial WP — Budget winter glove with waterproof membrane and decent insulation. Good for mild winter riding at accessible pricing.

If passive insulation is not enough, consider heated gloves or heated grips. The combination of insulated gloves plus heated grips is the ultimate cold-weather solution for British winter touring.

Hand Warming Tips

Wear silk liners underneath for an additional insulating layer. Use chemical hand warmers in gauntlets on the coldest days. Fit handlebar muffs if your bike allows them. Keep spare dry gloves in your luggage for when your main pair gets wet mid-tour.

Combining Heated Grips and Insulated Gloves

The ultimate cold-weather hand warming solution combines heated grips with insulated winter gloves. The grips warm your palms from below while the gloves insulate the backs of your hands and fingers from above. This dual approach lets you use thinner, more dexterous gloves than you would need with passive insulation alone. Many riders find that medium-weight three-season gloves combined with heated grips outperform the thickest winter gloves without heated grips, giving better control feel while maintaining warmth.

faq.q: Why do my hands get cold so fast?
faq.a: Your hands are fully exposed at the front of the bike gripping metal controls that conduct cold, and blood flow to the extremities reduces when your core temperature drops. Hands also have little insulating body fat. At motorway speeds in winter, wind chill can push the effective temperature below minus 10C, numbing fingers within minutes without proper insulation and wind blocking.

faq.q: What features matter most in winter gloves?
faq.a: Look for synthetic insulation like PrimaLoft or Thinsulate that stays warm when damp, a waterproof membrane such as Gore-Tex, and long gauntlets that seal over your jacket cuffs to stop wind tracking up your sleeves. Pre-curved fingers preserve dexterity in thick gloves, and a chamois or rubber visor wipe on the left index finger clears rain on the move.

faq.q: Are heated grips better than thick gloves?
faq.a: The best solution combines both. Heated grips warm your palms from below while insulated gloves protect the backs of your hands and fingers from above. This lets you use thinner, more dexterous gloves than passive insulation alone would allow. Many riders find medium-weight three-season gloves plus heated grips outperform the thickest winter gloves without grips, giving better control feel and warmth.

faq.q: How can I add extra warmth on the coldest days?
faq.a: Wear thin silk liners under your gloves for an additional insulating layer, and use chemical hand warmers inside the gauntlets on the coldest rides. Handlebar muffs, if your bike accepts them, dramatically cut wind chill. Always carry a spare dry pair of gloves in your luggage, because wet gloves lose their insulating value and leave your hands cold for the rest of the day.
